title: Rest and play
hook: holy leisure is part of the rule
tomorrow: who walks in with you when you're the new kid somewhere?

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: a portion, the widow's two coins, measured by the share. Today's piece of the rule costs nothing but time.

Two-a-days, a summer job, a phone that buzzes on vacation. Rest gets treated as what's left when the work runs out, and play as something you outgrow. So can a lazy afternoon be part of a holy life? Ask the first page of the Bible. Its first week doesn't end with one last job. It ends with a day off.
screen: `REST IS WHAT'S LEFT OVER?` → `CAN A LAZY AFTERNOON BE HOLY?` → `THE FIRST WEEK ENDS WITH A DAY OFF.`

segments.voice: Genesis says God "rested on the seventh day from all his work which he had done." Rest is built into creation, not earned after it. When the apostles come back so busy they haven't had time to eat, Jesus says: "Come apart into a desert place, and rest a little." Augustine had a name for it: holy leisure, the free time that love of truth goes looking for. And play? The prophet Zechariah pictures a city healed, and here's the sign: "the streets of the city shall be full of boys and girls, playing in the streets thereof." One to tell a friend: in that prophecy, kids playing in the street is what a restored city looks like. Here's something Catholics share with their Jewish neighbors. The Jewish Bible, in the JPS translation, says "Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy," and Isaiah asks Israel to "call the sabbath a delight." For Jews, Shabbat is a weekly gift, a delight and not a chore, and Catholics hear rest as a gift too. And one honest difference: Jews keep the seventh day, Shabbat, with its own laws and customs; Catholics keep Sunday, the day of the resurrection, as the Lord's day, setting aside work that crowds out worship, joy and rest. Two days, kept differently, and the same conviction: rest is holy.
screen: `HE RESTED ON THE SEVENTH DAY.` · `COME APART AND REST A LITTLE.` · `BOYS AND GIRLS, PLAYING.` · `SHABBAT AND SUNDAY.` · then, large: `HOLY LEISURE.`

segments.voice: Sit back. Drop your shoulders, unclench your jaw and your hands, the way you would on a slow afternoon with nothing due. If a task shows up in your head, set it down for later. When the time is up, put one block of rest on this week's calendar, and guard it like practice.
Rest and play. Time off that belongs in a holy life, from the first week of creation to kids playing in a healed city.
Your line: holy leisure. Rest is part of the rule, not a break from it. Go gently.
